title: Law & Justice
subtitle: Name the courts, defend a right and follow a trial in confident, precise French

lessons.title: Le système judiciaire français
lessons.description: How French courts are organised and who does what: juge, avocat, procureur, greffier and the famous jury populaire.

blocks.heading: Two orders, not one
blocks.body: French justice is split into two parallel worlds. "L'ordre judiciaire" settles disputes between private people (civil) and punishes offences (pénal); "l'ordre administratif" judges the State itself, through "les tribunaux administratifs" and, at the top, "le Conseil d'État". So if your neighbour floods your flat you go to "le tribunal judiciaire"; if a town hall refuses your building permit you go to "le tribunal administratif". English has no equivalent split, which is why "court" alone is never a safe translation.

examples.french: L'affaire relève de l'ordre judiciaire, pas de l'ordre administratif.
examples.english: The case falls under the judicial order, not the administrative one.
examples.note: "relever de" = to come under the jurisdiction of

examples.french: Il a saisi le tribunal administratif contre la préfecture.
examples.english: He took the prefecture to the administrative court.

examples.french: Le Conseil d'État a annulé le décret.
examples.english: The Conseil d'État struck down the decree.

examples.french: En matière pénale, c'est l'État qui poursuit.
examples.english: In criminal matters, it is the State that prosecutes.
examples.note: "en matière pénale / civile" is the standard formula

examples.french: Le Conseil constitutionnel vérifie la conformité des lois à la Constitution.
examples.english: The Constitutional Council checks that laws conform to the Constitution.

examples.french: Les deux ordres ne se confondent jamais.
examples.english: The two orders are never merged.

blocks.tip: "La cour" (with a lower-case c) is a courtyard; "la Cour" in legal French is a superior court — cour d'appel, cour d'assises, Cour de cassation.

blocks.heading: Who sits where
blocks.body: All French judges are "des magistrats", but they come in two families. "Les magistrats du siège" sit, listen and decide — that is "le juge". "Les magistrats du parquet" stand up to speak for society and demand a sentence — that is "le procureur". Around them, "l'avocat" defends a party, "le greffier" records everything, and "l'huissier" calls the case and later enforces the ruling.

examples.french: Le juge a demandé le silence dans la salle.
examples.english: The judge called for silence in the room.

examples.french: Le procureur de la République requiert cinq ans de prison.
examples.english: The public prosecutor is calling for five years in prison.
examples.note: "requérir" is the parquet's verb; a defence lawyer "plaide"

examples.french: Son avocate a été brillante à l'audience.
examples.english: Her lawyer was brilliant at the hearing.

examples.french: Le greffier note chaque déclaration au procès-verbal.
examples.english: The clerk records every statement in the official minutes.

examples.french: Les magistrats du siège sont inamovibles.
examples.english: Sitting judges cannot be removed from office.

examples.french: L'avocat s'est inscrit au barreau de Lyon.
examples.english: The lawyer joined the Lyon bar.

blocks.tip: Address a judge as « Monsieur le Président » / « Madame la Présidente », never « Monsieur le Juge » — that is a film cliché.

blocks.heading: From first instance to cassation
blocks.body: A case travels upwards. It starts "en première instance", can be re-judged completely "en appel" before "la cour d'appel", and finally reaches "la Cour de cassation", which judges only the law and not the facts. Serious crimes go to "la cour d'assises", the one court where ordinary citizens sit as "jurés" — the French jury is drawn by lot from the electoral roll and deliberates together with the professional judges.

examples.french: Elle a été condamnée en première instance, puis relaxée en appel.
examples.english: She was convicted at first instance, then cleared on appeal.

examples.french: La Cour de cassation ne rejuge pas les faits.
examples.english: The Court of Cassation does not re-judge the facts.

examples.french: Six jurés tirés au sort siègent aux assises.
examples.english: Six jurors drawn by lot sit in the assize court.
examples.note: "tirer au sort" = to draw by lot

examples.french: L'avocat a annoncé qu'il se pourvoyait en cassation.
examples.english: The lawyer announced he was appealing to the Court of Cassation.

examples.french: Le jugement a été cassé pour vice de procédure.
examples.english: The ruling was quashed for a procedural flaw.

examples.french: Un juré n'a pas le droit de parler du dossier à l'extérieur.
examples.english: A juror has no right to talk about the case outside.

blocks.tip: "Faire appel" = to appeal a decision. "Se pourvoir en cassation" is the last step — and it is not a third trial, only a check of legal reasoning.

blocks.heading: The passive voice, the language of institutions
blocks.body: Legal and administrative French loves the passive: it names the act, not the actor. Form it with "être" + past participle, and agree the participle with the subject. The agent, when given at all, follows "par": "jugé par le tribunal". With verbs of feeling or long-term states, the agent takes "de" instead: "respecté de tous". Notice that a French passive can only be built on a direct object — you cannot translate "he was given a fine" word for word; French says "on lui a infligé une amende".

examples.french: L'affaire a été jugée en première instance.
examples.english: The case was tried at first instance.

examples.french: Les deux prévenus ont été relaxés.
examples.english: The two defendants were cleared.

examples.french: Le décret a été annulé par le Conseil d'État.
examples.english: The decree was annulled by the Council of State.

examples.french: Ce magistrat est respecté de ses confrères.
examples.english: This judge is respected by his colleagues.

examples.french: Une amende lui a été infligée.
examples.english: A fine was imposed on him.

examples.french: La séance sera levée à dix-huit heures.
examples.english: The session will be adjourned at six p.m.

blocks.tip: In the press, "on" and the reflexive passive replace the heavy passive: "le dossier s'est réglé à l'amiable" sounds far more natural than "a été réglé".

blocks.heading: Relative pronouns for precise definitions
blocks.body: Defining who does what requires "qui" (subject), "que" (direct object), "dont" (replacing de + noun) and "auquel / à laquelle" (replacing à + noun). Legal French adds "lequel" after prepositions when the antecedent is a thing: "le texte sur lequel repose la décision". "Dont" is the one English speakers avoid, yet it is everywhere here: "un juge dont l'indépendance est garantie".

examples.french: Le magistrat qui préside l'audience s'appelle le président.
examples.english: The judge who chairs the hearing is called the president.

examples.french: L'avocate que vous avez consultée est spécialiste du droit du travail.
examples.english: The lawyer you consulted specialises in employment law.

examples.french: C'est un principe dont dépend tout le procès.
examples.english: It is a principle on which the whole trial depends.

examples.french: La juridiction à laquelle il s'est adressé n'était pas compétente.
examples.english: The court he applied to had no jurisdiction.

examples.french: Le texte sur lequel se fonde l'accusation date de 1994.
examples.english: The text on which the prosecution is based dates from 1994.

examples.french: Voici le dossier dont je vous ai parlé.
examples.english: Here is the file I told you about.

blocks.tip: After a preposition, use "qui" only for people ("l'avocat avec qui je travaille") and "lequel" for things ("la loi selon laquelle…").

items.prompt: Explain the split between the two orders.
items.french: Ce litige relève de l'ordre administratif, pas de l'ordre judiciaire.
items.english: This dispute comes under the administrative order, not the judicial one.
items.tip: "Relève" opens wide: ruh-LEV, not ruh-LEEV. Keep "ordre" as one beat, OR-druh, with a barely audible final -re.

items.prompt: Name the people in the room.
items.french: Le juge préside, le procureur requiert et l'avocat plaide.
items.english: The judge chairs, the prosecutor calls for a sentence and the lawyer pleads.
items.tip: "Requiert" is ruh-KYEHR — two syllables only, and the -t is silent. Don't say "ruh-kwee-EHR".

items.prompt: Use a relative pronoun with 'dont'.
items.french: C'est un principe dont dépend l'équilibre de tout le procès.
items.english: It is a principle on which the balance of the whole trial depends.
items.tip: "Dont" rhymes with "mont": nasal -on, no final t sound. Link it straight into "dépend" without a pause.

passages.title: Une journée au tribunal judiciaire
passages.french:
À neuf heures, la salle d'audience est déjà pleine, et personne n'a l'air d'y comprendre grand-chose.
Un huissier appelle les affaires les unes après les autres, d'une voix qui ne monte jamais.
Sur l'estrade, trois magistrats du siège s'installent ; en contrebas, le greffier ouvre son ordinateur et ne le quittera plus des yeux.
À droite, debout, le procureur représente la société : ce n'est pas lui qu'on juge, c'est lui qui accuse au nom de tous.
« Le public croit toujours que le procureur et le juge travaillent ensemble », soupire une avocate entre deux dossiers.
« Or le magistrat du parquet demande, et le magistrat du siège décide. Toute la différence est là. »
La première affaire dure onze minutes : un vol de téléphone, un prévenu qui reconnaît les faits, une amende.
La deuxième prend une heure, parce que la partie civile conteste le montant des dommages.
Les justiciables, eux, découvrent un vocabulaire dont personne ne leur a jamais expliqué le sens.
On leur parle de première instance, de renvoi, de délibéré, comme si ces mots allaient de soi.
À midi, la présidente annonce que le jugement sera rendu dans quinze jours et lève l'audience.
Dans le couloir, un homme demande à son avocat si tout cela signifie qu'il a gagné.
« Cela signifie qu'on attend », répond l'avocat, qui a l'habitude de la question.
Et il ajoute, en rangeant sa robe : « La justice est lente parce qu'elle écoute. C'est le prix. »
passages.english:
At nine o'clock, the courtroom is already full, and nobody seems to understand much of what is going on.
A bailiff calls the cases one after another, in a voice that never rises.
On the platform, three sitting judges settle in; below them, the clerk opens his computer and will not take his eyes off it again.
On the right, standing, the prosecutor represents society: he is not the one being judged, he is the one accusing in everyone's name.
"The public always thinks the prosecutor and the judge work together," sighs a lawyer between two files.
"But the prosecution judge asks, and the sitting judge decides. That is the whole difference."
The first case lasts eleven minutes: a stolen phone, a defendant who admits the facts, a fine.
The second takes an hour, because the civil party is disputing the amount of damages.
The people before the court, for their part, discover a vocabulary whose meaning nobody has ever explained to them.
They are told about first instance, postponement, deliberation, as if those words were self-evident.
At midday, the presiding judge announces that the ruling will be handed down in a fortnight and adjourns the hearing.
In the corridor, a man asks his lawyer whether all that means he has won.
"It means we wait," replies the lawyer, who is used to the question.
And he adds, putting away his gown: "Justice is slow because it listens. That is the price."

lessons.title: Les droits fondamentaux
lessons.description: Rights, freedoms and the constitutional vocabulary the French use to defend them — and to argue about their limits.

blocks.heading: Where French rights come from
blocks.body: The French Constitution of 1958 is short, so most rights live in what lawyers call "le bloc de constitutionnalité": the 1789 « Déclaration des droits de l'homme et du citoyen », the 1946 preamble and the Charter of the Environment. Note the vocabulary: a right is "reconnu" (recognised), then "garanti" (guaranteed), and finally "protégé" (protected) by a judge. If it is violated, French says "il y a atteinte à" or, more strongly, "ce droit est bafoué".

examples.french: La liberté d'expression est garantie par la Constitution.
examples.english: Freedom of expression is guaranteed by the Constitution.

examples.french: La Déclaration de 1789 fait toujours partie de notre droit positif.
examples.english: The 1789 Declaration is still part of our law in force.

examples.french: Cette mesure porte atteinte à la vie privée des salariés.
examples.english: This measure infringes employees' privacy.

examples.french: Dans plusieurs pays, ce droit est ouvertement bafoué.
examples.english: In several countries, this right is openly flouted.

examples.french: Le préambule de 1946 reconnaît le droit de grève.
examples.english: The 1946 preamble recognises the right to strike.

examples.french: Nul ne peut être privé arbitrairement de sa liberté.
examples.english: No one may be arbitrarily deprived of their liberty.
examples.note: « nul ne » is the formal legal negation

blocks.tip: "Le droit" without an article-plus-complement means law as a field ("étudier le droit"); "un droit" is an individual entitlement; "les droits" can also mean fees — "les droits d'inscription".

blocks.heading: Freedom is always plural
blocks.body: French rarely says "la liberté" alone in a debate; it names which one. "La liberté d'expression", "de la presse", "de conscience", "de circulation", "de réunion", "d'association". Each is defended and each is limited — and the standard formula for the limit is that a freedom stops "là où commence celle des autres". The three republican words "liberté, égalité, fraternité" complete the set, joined in modern debate by "la laïcité" and "la dignité".

examples.french: La liberté de la presse est un contre-pouvoir essentiel.
examples.english: Freedom of the press is an essential check on power.

examples.french: La liberté de conscience protège les croyants comme les athées.
examples.english: Freedom of conscience protects believers and atheists alike.

examples.french: La laïcité n'est pas l'hostilité aux religions, mais la neutralité de l'État.
examples.english: Secularism is not hostility to religions, but the neutrality of the State.

examples.french: Ma liberté s'arrête là où commence celle des autres.
examples.english: My freedom ends where other people's begins.

examples.french: Le droit de manifester découle de la liberté de réunion.
examples.english: The right to demonstrate derives from freedom of assembly.

examples.french: La dignité de la personne humaine est un principe à valeur constitutionnelle.
examples.english: Human dignity is a principle of constitutional value.

blocks.tip: Careful with false friends: "la liberté surveillée" is probation, and "mettre en liberté" means to release from custody, not to set free in general.

blocks.heading: Arguing about limits
blocks.body: At B2 the interesting move is not listing rights but weighing them. French debate uses a stable set of connectors for that: "certes… mais", "bien que" + subjunctive, "au nom de", "au détriment de", "un juste équilibre entre". The recurring question is whether a restriction is "proportionnée" and "justifiée", or whether it constitutes "une dérive" — a slide towards abuse.

examples.french: Certes, la sécurité compte, mais pas au détriment des libertés.
examples.english: Security matters, of course, but not at the expense of freedoms.

examples.french: Bien que la mesure soit temporaire, elle inquiète les associations.
examples.english: Although the measure is temporary, it worries campaign groups.

examples.french: On restreint des droits au nom de l'ordre public.
examples.english: Rights are being restricted in the name of public order.

examples.french: Il faut trouver un juste équilibre entre transparence et vie privée.
examples.english: A fair balance must be found between transparency and privacy.

examples.french: Cette restriction n'est ni nécessaire ni proportionnée.
examples.english: This restriction is neither necessary nor proportionate.

examples.french: Beaucoup dénoncent une dérive sécuritaire.
examples.english: Many are denouncing a slide towards a security state.

blocks.tip: "Au nom de" is the giveaway of a contested justification: whoever uses it usually intends to challenge the reason, not endorse it.

blocks.heading: Concession: bien que, quoique, même si
blocks.body: Conceding a point before rebutting it is the core B2 debating move. "Bien que" and "quoique" take the subjunctive: "bien que la mesure soit légale…". "Même si" and "alors que" take the indicative: "même si la mesure est légale…". A shortcut used constantly in the press is "certes… mais": you grant the objection in one clause and demolish it in the next. Never write "malgré que" — it is considered incorrect; use "malgré" + noun instead.

examples.french: Bien que le texte soit constitutionnel, il reste contesté.
examples.english: Although the text is constitutional, it remains contested.

examples.french: Quoiqu'elle ait raison sur le fond, sa méthode dérange.
examples.english: Although she is right on the substance, her method is unsettling.

examples.french: Même si la loi le permet, ce n'est pas légitime.
examples.english: Even if the law allows it, it is not legitimate.

examples.french: Certes, la sécurité est un droit ; mais elle n'annule pas les autres.
examples.english: Security is a right, certainly; but it does not cancel out the others.

examples.french: Malgré les critiques, le décret a été maintenu.
examples.english: Despite the criticism, the decree was maintained.

examples.french: Il a signé, alors qu'il savait le texte fragile.
examples.english: He signed, even though he knew the text was shaky.

blocks.tip: "Quoique" (one word) = although. "Quoi que" (two words) = whatever: « quoi qu'il dise, personne ne le croit ».

blocks.heading: Impersonal formulas of obligation and right
blocks.body: Legal French almost never says "you must". It uses impersonal structures: "il est interdit de", "nul ne peut", "il convient de", "chacun a le droit de", "toute personne a droit à". Note the two patterns with "droit": "avoir le droit DE + infinitive" (to be allowed to do) versus "avoir droit À + noun" (to be entitled to something). Mixing them up is the single most common B2 error in this field.

examples.english: No one may be arbitrarily detained.

passages.title: Jusqu'où va une liberté ?
passages.french:
On répète volontiers que la liberté des uns s'arrête là où commence celle des autres, comme si la frontière était tracée d'avance.
Elle ne l'est jamais : c'est précisément le travail du juge que de la tracer, affaire après affaire.
Prenez la liberté d'expression, garantie depuis 1789 et pourtant limitée dès la première ligne de la loi de 1881 sur la presse.
On peut critiquer un ministre, ridiculiser une croyance, publier une enquête gênante ; on ne peut ni diffamer, ni injurier, ni appeler à la haine.
La distinction paraît simple sur le papier, elle est redoutable dans la salle d'audience.
« Le juge ne se demande pas si le propos est choquant », explique une professeure de droit public.
« Il se demande s'il vise des idées ou des personnes. Choquer reste un droit ; désigner quelqu'un à la vindicte n'en est pas un. »
Même logique pour la liberté de circulation, suspendue pendant les confinements au nom de la santé publique.
Le Conseil d'État a rappelé qu'une restriction n'est acceptable que si elle est nécessaire, adaptée et proportionnée : trois mots, trois verrous.
Bien qu'elle soit invoquée en permanence, la proportionnalité reste mal comprise du grand public, qui y voit une formule de juriste.
C'est pourtant elle qui empêche l'exception de devenir la règle.
Car le vrai risque n'est pas la loi brutale que tout le monde verrait passer.
C'est l'accumulation de petites mesures raisonnables, chacune justifiée, dont la somme finit par dessiner un autre régime.
« On ne perd pas ses libertés d'un coup, conclut la juriste. On les perd par consentement, une dérogation à la fois. »
passages.english:
People readily repeat that one person's freedom stops where another's begins, as if the border had been drawn in advance.
It never is: drawing it, case after case, is precisely the judge's job.
Take freedom of expression, guaranteed since 1789 and yet limited from the very first line of the 1881 press law.
You may criticise a minister, ridicule a belief, publish an awkward investigation; you may not defame, insult, or call for hatred.
The distinction looks simple on paper; it is formidable in the courtroom.
"The judge does not ask whether the remark is shocking," explains a professor of public law.
"He asks whether it targets ideas or people. Shocking remains a right; singling someone out for a mob does not."
The same logic applies to freedom of movement, suspended during the lockdowns in the name of public health.
The Council of State recalled that a restriction is acceptable only if it is necessary, appropriate and proportionate: three words, three locks.
Although it is invoked constantly, proportionality remains poorly understood by the general public, who see it as lawyers' jargon.
Yet it is what stops the exception from becoming the rule.
Because the real risk is not the brutal law that everyone would see coming.
It is the accumulation of small reasonable measures, each one justified, whose sum ends up sketching a different regime.
"You do not lose your freedoms all at once," the legal scholar concludes. "You lose them by consent, one exemption at a time."

lessons.title: Un procès
lessons.description: Courtroom language from the opening of the hearing to the verdict, and how to report what witnesses said.

blocks.heading: The choreography of a hearing
blocks.body: A French trial follows a fixed sequence, and each stage has its verb. The accused "comparaît" before the court; the president "ouvre l'audience" and "procède à l'interrogatoire"; witnesses "prêtent serment" then "déposent"; the prosecutor delivers "le réquisitoire"; the defence gives "la plaidoirie"; the accused has "le dernier mot"; the court "se retire pour délibérer" and finally "rend son verdict".

examples.french: L'accusé comparaît détenu depuis février.
examples.english: The accused has been appearing in custody since February.

examples.french: L'audience est ouverte.
examples.english: The hearing is now open.

examples.french: Le témoin prête serment de dire toute la vérité.
examples.english: The witness swears to tell the whole truth.

examples.french: Après le réquisitoire, l'avocate a plaidé pendant deux heures.
examples.english: After the closing speech for the prosecution, the lawyer pleaded for two hours.

examples.french: La cour se retire pour délibérer.
examples.english: The court withdraws to deliberate.

examples.french: Le verdict sera rendu en fin de soirée.
examples.english: The verdict will be delivered late this evening.

blocks.tip: « La parole est à la défense » is the exact phrase used to hand over to the lawyer. « L'audience est suspendue » announces a break; « levée » means it is over.

blocks.heading: Saying what happened — and how sure you are
blocks.body: Testimony lives on degrees of certainty. French marks them precisely: "j'affirme que" (I state), "je maintiens que" (I stand by), "il me semble que" (it seems to me), "je crois me souvenir que" (I think I remember), "je ne saurais dire" (I couldn't say). Denial has its own scale too: "je nie les faits", "je conteste cette version", "je reconnais les faits mais je conteste l'intention".

examples.french: J'affirme que je n'ai jamais rencontré cet homme.
examples.english: I state that I have never met this man.

examples.french: Je maintiens ma déclaration du 12 mars.
examples.english: I stand by my statement of 12 March.

examples.french: Il me semble qu'il portait un manteau sombre.
examples.english: It seems to me that he was wearing a dark coat.

examples.french: Je crois me souvenir qu'il était vingt-deux heures.
examples.english: I think I remember it was ten p.m.

examples.french: Je reconnais les faits, mais je conteste la préméditation.
examples.english: I admit the facts, but I dispute the premeditation.

examples.french: Je ne saurais dire combien de temps cela a duré.
examples.english: I could not say how long it lasted.
examples.note: "je ne saurais" = formal, softened "je ne peux pas"

blocks.tip: Perjury is « le faux témoignage » and it is a criminal offence — which is why witnesses hedge so carefully rather than guess.

blocks.heading: Verdict and sentence
blocks.body: Two families of outcome. Cleared: "relaxé" before a tribunal correctionnel, "acquitté" before a cour d'assises — the words are not interchangeable. Convicted: "condamné à" + the penalty, which may be "une amende", "une peine de prison ferme", "avec sursis", or "des travaux d'intérêt général". Whatever the outcome, either side may "faire appel" within ten days.

examples.french: Le prévenu a été relaxé faute de preuves.
examples.english: The defendant was cleared for lack of evidence.

examples.french: L'accusé a été acquitté par la cour d'assises.
examples.english: The accused was acquitted by the assize court.

examples.french: Il a été condamné à deux ans, dont un avec sursis.
examples.english: He was sentenced to two years, one of them suspended.
examples.note: "dont un avec sursis" is the standard press formula

examples.french: La peine est assortie d'une amende de cinq mille euros.
examples.english: The sentence comes with a five-thousand-euro fine.

examples.french: Le parquet a aussitôt fait appel du jugement.
examples.english: The prosecution immediately appealed the ruling.

examples.french: La présomption d'innocence vaut jusqu'à la condamnation définitive.
examples.english: The presumption of innocence holds until the conviction is final.

blocks.tip: In French, an ongoing case takes « présumé » before the noun: « le meurtrier présumé ». Dropping it in writing can itself be legally risky.

blocks.heading: Reported speech: the tense shift
blocks.body: Reporting testimony means moving the whole sentence back one step in time. Présent becomes imparfait, passé composé becomes plus-que-parfait, futur becomes conditionnel présent, futur antérieur becomes conditionnel passé. The imparfait, plus-que-parfait and conditionnel do not move — they are already "backshifted". Time words shift too: "hier" becomes "la veille", "demain" becomes "le lendemain", "maintenant" becomes "à ce moment-là".

examples.french: « Je connais cet homme. » → Il a déclaré qu'il connaissait cet homme.
examples.english: "I know this man." → He stated that he knew this man.

examples.french: « J'ai vu la voiture. » → Elle a affirmé qu'elle avait vu la voiture.
examples.english: "I saw the car." → She stated that she had seen the car.

examples.french: « Je porterai plainte. » → Il a annoncé qu'il porterait plainte.
examples.english: "I will file a complaint." → He announced that he would file a complaint.

examples.french: « Je suis arrivé hier. » → Il a expliqué qu'il était arrivé la veille.
examples.english: "I arrived yesterday." → He explained that he had arrived the day before.

examples.french: « Nous partirons demain. » → Ils ont dit qu'ils partiraient le lendemain.
examples.english: "We will leave tomorrow." → They said they would leave the next day.

examples.french: « Je ne me souviens pas. » → Le témoin a répondu qu'il ne se souvenait pas.
examples.english: "I don't remember." → The witness replied that he did not remember.

blocks.tip: If the reporting verb is in the present (« il dit que… »), nothing shifts. The whole mechanism only kicks in after a past reporting verb.

blocks.heading: Reporting questions and orders
blocks.body: Questions lose their inversion and their question mark. "Est-ce que" and inversion both become "si": « Étiez-vous là ? » → il a demandé si j'étais là. "Qu'est-ce que" becomes "ce que", "qu'est-ce qui" becomes "ce qui"; other question words (où, quand, pourquoi, comment) stay as they are. Orders become "de" + infinitive: « Répondez ! » → le président lui a ordonné de répondre.

examples.french: « Êtes-vous d'accord ? » → Il a demandé si j'étais d'accord.
examples.english: "Do you agree?" → He asked whether I agreed.

examples.french: « Qu'est-ce que vous avez vu ? » → Il a voulu savoir ce que j'avais vu.
examples.english: "What did you see?" → He wanted to know what I had seen.

examples.french: « Qu'est-ce qui s'est passé ? » → Elle a demandé ce qui s'était passé.
examples.english: "What happened?" → She asked what had happened.

examples.french: « Où étiez-vous ce soir-là ? » → On lui a demandé où il était ce soir-là.
examples.english: "Where were you that evening?" → He was asked where he was that evening.

examples.french: « Taisez-vous ! » → Le président lui a ordonné de se taire.
examples.english: "Be quiet!" → The presiding judge ordered him to be quiet.

examples.french: « Ne mentez pas. » → L'avocat lui a conseillé de ne pas mentir.
examples.english: "Don't lie." → The lawyer advised him not to lie.
examples.note: negation stays in front of the infinitive: de ne pas mentir

blocks.tip: Courtroom reports lean on precise verbs rather than "dire": déclarer, affirmer, reconnaître, contester, nier, préciser. Each already carries the speaker's stance.

items.prompt: Testify with a careful degree of certainty.
items.french: Je crois me souvenir qu'il portait un manteau sombre.
items.english: I think I remember that he was wearing a dark coat.
items.tip: Keep "crois me souvenir" as one smooth group: krwah-muh-soo-vuh-NEER. Hesitating there sounds like doubt about the truth, not about the memory.

items.prompt: Report a witness's statement.
items.french: Le témoin a déclaré qu'il n'avait jamais rencontré l'accusé.
items.english: The witness stated that he had never met the accused.
items.tip: "N'avait" contracts to nah-VEH — the ne is barely there but the vowel of avait stays open. Don't say nah-VAY.

items.prompt: Announce a sentence like a news anchor.
items.french: Le tribunal l'a condamné à trois ans, dont deux avec sursis.
items.english: The court sentenced him to three years, two of them suspended.
items.tip: "Sursis" ends on a hissed -ee: sür-SEE, final s silent. Round your lips hard for the ü of the first syllable.

passages.title: Le troisième jour du procès
passages.french:
L'audience reprend à quatorze heures et, pour la première fois depuis lundi, l'accusé accepte de parler.
La présidente lui rappelle qu'il n'est pas obligé de répondre et que son silence ne saurait être retenu contre lui.
Il déclare pourtant qu'il veut « rétablir les faits », et la salle se tait d'un coup.
Interrogé sur la soirée du 14, il répond qu'il était chez sa sœur et qu'il en était reparti vers minuit.
Le procureur lui fait observer que sa sœur, entendue la veille, avait situé son départ deux heures plus tôt.
« Elle s'est trompée », répond l'accusé, sans hésiter.
On appelle alors le témoin suivant, un voisin qui prête serment d'une voix mal assurée.
Il explique qu'il a entendu des cris, qu'il a d'abord cru à une dispute ordinaire, et qu'il n'a appelé la police qu'un quart d'heure plus tard.
L'avocate de la défense lui demande s'il a vu quelqu'un sortir de l'immeuble ; il reconnaît que non.
Elle insiste : a-t-il reconnu une voix ? Il hésite longuement, puis admet qu'il ne saurait le dire.
Dans son réquisitoire, le procureur parlera d'un faisceau d'indices concordants ; la défense, elle, plaidera le doute.
Car en droit français, le doute profite toujours à l'accusé, et la présidente le rappellera aux jurés avant qu'ils ne se retirent.
À dix-neuf heures, la cour part délibérer sans annoncer d'horaire.
Dans le couloir, personne ne parle : chacun sait que ces heures-là décident d'une vie entière.
passages.english:
The hearing resumes at two p.m. and, for the first time since Monday, the accused agrees to speak.
The presiding judge reminds him that he is not obliged to answer and that his silence cannot be held against him.
He states nonetheless that he wants to "set the facts straight", and the room falls silent at once.
Questioned about the evening of the 14th, he answers that he was at his sister's and that he left there around midnight.
The prosecutor points out to him that his sister, heard the day before, had put his departure two hours earlier.
"She got it wrong," the accused replies, without hesitating.
The next witness is then called, a neighbour who takes the oath in an unsteady voice.
He explains that he heard shouting, that he first thought it was an ordinary argument, and that he only called the police a quarter of an hour later.
The defence lawyer asks him whether he saw anyone leaving the building; he admits that he did not.
She presses on: did he recognise a voice? He hesitates for a long time, then admits that he could not say.
In his closing speech, the prosecutor will speak of a body of matching clues; the defence, for its part, will plead doubt.
Because in French law, doubt always benefits the accused, and the presiding judge will remind the jurors of that before they withdraw.
At seven p.m., the court goes off to deliberate without announcing a timetable.
In the corridor, nobody speaks: everyone knows that those hours decide an entire life.
